title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
specialty: Internal Medicine, Respiratory Medicine and Infectious Diseases

evidenceAudit.scope: Immunocompetent adults with CAP. Antibiotic regimens follow the Saudi MOH LRTI protocol (adopted from ATS/IDSA 2019); steroid and duration updates from ATS 2025.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Local formulary availability and hospital protocol adoption

pathophysiology.summary: CAP is acute infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside hospital. Alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate, causing consolidation, impaired gas exchange and, in severe cases, sepsis and respiratory failure.
keyMechanisms: Organisms reach the alveoli (usually by micro-aspiration) and overwhelm local defences; the inflammatory exudate fills air spaces (consolidation).
Ventilation–perfusion mismatch from consolidated lung causes hypoxaemia and tachypnoea.
The systemic inflammatory response can progress to sepsis, septic shock and multi-organ failure.
Resistant organisms (MRSA, Pseudomonas) are more likely after recent hospitalisation and IV antibiotics or with prior respiratory isolation.
Viral infection (e.g. influenza) can coexist with bacterial infection.

symptoms: Cough, sputum, fever, rigors, breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain.
physicalSigns: Fever (or hypothermia below 36 °C in severe disease), tachypnoea, tachycardia, hypoxia.
Focal crackles, bronchial breathing, dullness to percussion.
redFlags: ATS major criteria: septic shock needing vasopressors, or respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation — direct ICU admission

Three or more ATS minor criteria: RR 30 or more, PaO2/FiO2 250 or less, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, urea (BUN) 20 mg/dL or more (about 7 mmol/L), WBC below 4 × 10⁹/L, platelets below 100 × 10⁹/L, temperature below 36 °C, hypotension needing aggressive fluids

differentials.condition: Acute bronchitis or viral upper respiratory infection

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Pleuritic pain and hypoxia without consolidation; VTE risk factors.
Bilateral infiltrates, raised JVP, cardiomegaly, raised natriuretic peptide.
Subacute course, weight loss, upper-lobe or cavitary change; MOH protocol cautions against fluoroquinolones without excluding TB.
Onset 48 h or more after admission; follow the HAP/VAP section and local antibiogram.

ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Confirms CAP; antibiotics are started in clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed CAP. ATS 2025: lung ultrasound is an acceptable alternative where expertise exists.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and place of care
actions: Calculate PSI (MOH): class II (70 points or less) outpatient; III (71–90) outpatient or observation; IV (91–130) admit; V (above 130) admit to ICU.
Apply ATS severe CAP criteria: 1 major or 3 or more minor criteria = severe CAP.

clinicalManagement.title: Start empirical antibiotics (MOH protocol)
actions: Previously healthy outpatient: amoxicillin 1 g PO every 8 h for 5–7 days (or a macrolide or doxycycline as listed).
Outpatient with comorbidity or recent antibiotics: beta-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate, amoxicillin or cefuroxime) PLUS a macrolide.
Inpatient non-severe: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 h PLUS clarithromycin 500 mg every 12 h or azithromycin 500 mg then 250 mg daily (days 2–5).
Inpatient severe: ceftriaxone 1–2 g IV every 24 h PLUS a macrolide, or PLUS levofloxacin 750 mg IV every 24 h or moxifloxacin 400 mg IV every 24 h.

branches.condition: Prior MRSA isolation, or recent hospitalisation + IV antibiotics + validated local MRSA risk
actions: Add vancomycin 25–30 mg/kg IV loading (if acutely severe) then 1 g every 8 h, or linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 h.

branches.condition: Prior Pseudomonas isolation, or recent hospitalisation + IV antibiotics + local risk
actions: Replace the beta-lactam with piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 h, cefepime 2 g every 8 h, ceftazidime 2 g every 8 h, aztreonam 2 g every 8 h, meropenem 1 g every 8 h or imipenem 500 mg every 6 h.
Levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily; exclude TB first (MOH).
Oseltamivir 75 mg every 12 h for 5 days, plus standard antibacterial therapy.

clinicalManagement.title: Supportive care
actions: Oxygen to target saturations; fluids and vasopressors per sepsis guidance if shocked.

Steroids (ATS 2025): suggest systemic corticosteroids in severe CAP inpatients (stronger case if started within 24 h of meeting severe criteria, ICU admission or respiratory failure); do NOT give in non-severe CAP. Not recommended for confirmed influenza.

clinicalManagement.title: Duration and stopping
actions: Stop when clinically stable: afebrile 48–72 h, no supplemental oxygen (unless needed before), and no more than one instability sign (HR above 100, RR above 24, SBP 90 or less).
ATS 2025: non-severe inpatients and outpatients — less than 5 days (minimum 3) once stable; severe CAP — 5 days or more.
MOH regimens list 5–7 days for most agents; de-escalate on culture results.
No routine follow-up chest imaging in improving patients (ATS 2019).

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage community-acquired pneumonia in the emergency department.

keyPoints: Confirm with imaging; grade with PSI and ATS severe criteria.
Inpatient: ceftriaxone + macrolide; severe: ceftriaxone + macrolide or respiratory quinolone.
Add MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only with prior isolation or validated risk.
Stop once stable: short courses are enough.
pitfalls: Waiting for procalcitonin before treating confirmed CAP.
Routine follow-up chest X-ray in recovered patients.

patientEducation: Complete the antibiotic course; return if breathlessness, chest pain or confusion worsen.
Smoking cessation; influenza and pneumococcal vaccination.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: ICU for severe CAP with major criteria.
Respiratory or infectious diseases if not improving or resistant organisms.
dischargeCriteria: Clinically stable (afebrile, off oxygen or at baseline, at most one instability sign).
Able to take oral antibiotics and fluids.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review if not improving within 48–72 h. No routine follow-up chest X-ray; consider lung cancer screening where eligible (ATS 2019).
